article.title: Questions to Ask Before Hiring an Injury Attorney
article.author: Tiqua Jackson
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Finding the Right Personal Injury Lawyer After an Out-of-State Accident After an accident away from home, you may be dealing with an unfamiliar insurer, medical bills from another state, and questions about where to find a lawyer. The nearest office may not be the right place to start. Focus your search on these checks: Check authorization. Verify the attorney's licensing and ask how they would be authorized to handle your case. Test relevant experience. Use the first conversation to learn how the lawyer handles cases like yours. Understand the agreement. Get fee and expense terms in writing before you sign. This guide provides general information, not advice about your case. An appropriately authorized attorney can review your circumstances. Find Someone Who Can Handle the Case Where It Belongs If you were injured in another state, ask where your claim could be brought, which rules apply, and who may represent you there. Your home address alone won't answer those questions. Start with the location of the accident. Ask whether the claim could be brought in that state and what other locations might be available. For example, Michigan Legal Center's October 2026 explanation says whether a particular Michigan court can hear a case depends on the claim and the defendant's connections to Michigan. That example illustrates why a lawyer needs to review more than where you live. For an accident in New Jersey, an NJ injury lawyer such as Garces, Grabler & LeBrocq is an option to research. Confirm who would handle the matter and whether that attorney is authorized to appear in the relevant court. The firm lists motor vehicle accidents, truck accidents, and workers' compensation among its practice areas. Ask which type of claim fits your circumstances. Check the individual attorney. An office address alone doesn't establish whether the lawyer handling your file can appear in the relevant court. Look the individual up in that state's official directory. Maryland's attorney listing treats active status as good standing and authorization to practice, and the State Bar of Texas shows any public disciplinary history on each attorney's online profile. Licensing status doesn't establish experience with your type of claim. A lawyer licensed elsewhere may sometimes participate by working with a locally admitted lawyer who actively participates. The ABA model rules describe a conditional route for temporary legal services, but current state rules control. Ask how the proposed arrangement would work and whether separate court approval is needed. Request a deadline review early. Maryland has a default three-year filing period for civil actions at law, subject to other Code provisions. That rule does not establish the deadline for an out-of-state accident. Ask an attorney to identify when your filing period begins and which deadlines apply. Use the First Conversation to Test the Fit Use the consultation to learn how the lawyer would approach your claim and whether their working style suits your needs. Bring questions and take notes so you can compare the answers afterward. Bring a useful file. Gather a short timeline, photographs, witness names and contact details, the report number, insurance correspondence, and whatever medical and wage records you have so far. If you exchanged insurance details with the other driver at the scene, include those as well. Ask about cases like yours. Ask how often the attorney handles your type of accident, how they approach disputed responsibility, and what evidence they would gather. Ask what information they need before discussing a possible recovery. If your injuries are severe, ask about experience with long-term care needs. For serious injuries in Texas, Stogner Trial Law describes its catastrophic-injury category as life-altering injuries requiring extensive medical care and long-term support. Notice how answers are given. Ask who will handle the matter, how updates work, and what you can do from home rather than in person. Texas Court Help notes that one of a lawyer's most important duties is keeping the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter. Follow up by asking whom to contact with questions and how to send new records. Write down the proposed communication arrangements. Know What You Are Agreeing To Under a contingency-fee arrangement, the attorney's fee depends on a recovery. Expenses may be handled separately, so review both in the written agreement. Separate fees from expenses. The attorney's fee is one item; litigation expenses, such as records requests and expert reports, are another. Ask whether medical liens, or claims for repayment of medical costs, could also reduce what you receive. Review any firm's written agreement for the percentage and expense terms that would apply to your case. Texas Disciplinary Rule 1.04(d) requires contingent-fee agreements to be in writing and to state whether expenses are deducted before or after the fee is calculated. The order affects your share. Ask which method applies, what the percentage is, and whether it changes if the case goes to trial. Confirm the scope. Ask who is responsible for the case, whether another firm or local counsel may participate, and what work is included. If you are considering a firm for a serious injury claim, ask it to explain how its contingency arrangement applies to your matter, what case expenses you may owe, and who would handle the work. Use the same questions with every firm you compare. Read before signing. The ABA model fee rule calls for a written contingent-fee agreement signed by the client, though current state rules govern. Ask for explanations of any terms you don't understand, including what expenses, if any, you could owe without a recovery. Get the agreement in writing and keep a copy for your records. The same care applies later in the claim. Accepting a settlement usually means signing a release that bars future claims tied to the accident, so take your time with any offer and keep your statements to insurers calm and factual before agreeing to a number. Conclusion The right lawyer after an out-of-state accident is the one who can work where your claim belongs, has handled cases like yours, and explains the agreement clearly. Start by confirming that the attorney is authorized in the state where your case would be heard, then use the consultation to compare how each lawyer would approach your claim and keep you informed. Before you sign, make sure the fee percentage, the expense terms, and the people handling your file are all set out in writing. Taking those steps early protects your filing deadline and puts you in a stronger position for the rest of the claim. Frequently Asked Questions Do I need a lawyer licensed in the state where the accident happened? Usually, the attorney who appears in court on your claim needs to be authorized in that state. A lawyer licensed elsewhere may sometimes take part by working with a locally admitted lawyer, but each state's rules decide when that is allowed. Ask any firm you speak with how it would be authorized to handle your case. How do personal injury lawyers charge for their work? Many work on a contingency basis, which means the fee depends on a recovery. Case expenses, such as records requests and expert reports, may be handled separately. The written agreement should explain the percentage, how expenses are treated, and what you could owe if there is no recovery. What should I bring to a first consultation? Bring a short timeline of the accident, photographs, witness contact details, the police report number, insurance correspondence, and any medical and wage records you have. A complete file helps the lawyer assess your claim and gives you a fair basis for comparing firms. How long do I have to file a personal injury claim? Filing deadlines vary by state and by type of claim. Maryland's default period for civil actions at law is three years, and Texas generally allows two years from the date of injury for personal injury lawsuits. Because other rules can change the deadline, ask an attorney to confirm when your filing period begins. Should I accept the insurance company's first settlement offer? Take time to review any offer before agreeing to it. A settlement usually comes with a release that ends future claims tied to the accident, even if your injuries later turn out to be more serious. Make sure you understand the full extent of your losses before you sign.
